column2: When early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
the sacred might of Alcinous rose from his bed,
and Zeus-born Odysseus, sacker of cities, rose.
And for them the sacred might of Alcinous led the way
to the assembly of the Phaeacians, which had been made for them by the ships.
Coming there they sat down on polished stones
close by. And through the city went Pallas Athena,
likened to the herald of prudent Alcinous,
planning a return for great-hearted Odysseus,
and standing beside each man she spoke a word:

Come, leaders and counsellors of the Phaeacians,
12	go to the assembly, that you may learn of the stranger,
13	who has newly come to the house of prudent Alcinous
14	after wandering over the sea, in form like the immortals.
So saying she roused the might and spirit of each.
Quickly the assembly places and the seats were filled
with men gathering; and many marvelled, seeing
the prudent son of Laertes; and on him Athena
poured marvellous grace over his head and shoulders
and made him taller and stouter to look upon,
so that he might be dear to all the Phaeacians
and awesome and revered, and might accomplish the many
contests with which the Phaeacians would test Odysseus.
But when they were gathered and assembled together,
Alcinous spoke out and said among them:

Hear me, leaders and counsellors of the Phaeacians,
27	that I may say what the heart in my breast bids me.
28	This stranger, I do not know who, has come wandering to my house,
29	either from men of the dawn or of the evening;
30	he urges an escort, and entreats that it be made sure.
31	So let us, as before, speed on an escort.
32	For not even any other, whoever comes to my house,
33	stays here long lamenting for want of an escort.
34	But come, let us draw a black ship down to the divine sea,
35	on her first voyage, and let fifty-two youths
36	be chosen from the district, those who are best of old.
37	And binding the oars well to the thole-pins, all of you
38	disembark; and then prepare a quick meal,
39	coming to our house; and I will provide well for all.
40	To the young men I give these orders; but you others,
41	sceptre-holding kings, come to my fair house,
42	that we may entertain the stranger in the halls,
43	and let no one refuse. And call the divine singer
44	Demodocus; for the god gave him song beyond others
45	to delight, whichever way his spirit urges him to sing.
So speaking he led the way, and the sceptre-holders followed
together; and the herald went for the divine singer.
And the fifty-two chosen youths
went, as he ordered, to the shore of the unharvested sea.
But when they had come down to the ship and the sea,
they drew the black ship down into the depth of the sea,
and put in mast and sails in the black ship,
and fitted the oars in leather thongs,
all in due order, and spread out the white sails.
They moored her high in the roadstead; and then
they went to the great house of prudent Alcinous.
And the porticoes and courts and rooms were filled with men
gathering; and many there were, young and old.
For them Alcinous sacrificed twelve sheep,
eight white-tusked swine, and two shambling oxen;
these they flayed and dressed, and prepared a lovely feast.
And the herald came near leading the beloved singer,
whom the Muse loved above others, and gave him both good and evil;
she took away his eyes, but gave him sweet song.
For him Pontonous set a silver-studded chair
in the midst of the banqueters, leaning it against a tall pillar;
and from a peg he hung the clear-toned lyre
just above his head, and showed him with his hands how to take it,
the herald; and beside him he set a basket and a fair table,
and beside it a cup of wine, to drink when his spirit bade.
And they stretched out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
But when they had put away the desire for drink and food,
the Muse moved the singer to sing the famous deeds of men,
from a song whose fame then reached the broad heaven,
the quarrel of Odysseus and Achilles son of Peleus,
how once they contended at a rich feast of the gods
with dreadful words, and Agamemnon, lord of men,
rejoiced in his mind that the best of the Achaeans were contending.
For so Phoebus Apollo had told him in prophecy
in holy Pytho, when he crossed the stone threshold
to consult; for then the beginning of woe was rolling
upon Trojans and Danaans through the counsels of great Zeus.
This the far-famed singer sang; but Odysseus,
taking his great purple cloak in his stout hands,
drew it down over his head, and covered his fair face;
for he was ashamed before the Phaeacians, shedding tears from under his brows.
Indeed, whenever the divine singer ceased his singing,
he would wipe away the tear and take the cloak from his head,
and taking a two-handled cup he would pour a libation to the gods;
but whenever he began again and the nobles urged him to sing,
the best of the Phaeacians, since they took delight in his words,
again Odysseus, covering his head, would groan.
Then from all the others he escaped notice shedding tears,
but Alcinous alone noticed him and observed,
sitting near him, and heard him groaning heavily.
At once he spoke among the Phaeacians, lovers of oars:

Hear me, leaders and counsellors of the Phaeacians.
98	Already we have our fill of the feast, which suits every heart,
99	and of the lyre, which is the companion of the rich feast;
100	now let us go out and try ourselves in contests
101	of all kinds, that the stranger may tell his friends,
102	returning home, how far we excel others
103	in boxing and wrestling and leaping and in running.
So speaking he led the way, and they followed together.
And the herald hung the clear-toned lyre from its peg,
and took Demodocus by the hand and led him out of the hall,
and led him by the same road which the others took,
the best of the Phaeacians, to marvel at the contests.
They went to the assembly, and a great throng followed,
countless; and many good young men stood up.
Up rose Acroneus and Ocyalus and Elatreus,
Nauteus and Prymneus and Anchialus and Eretmeus,
Ponteus and Proreus, Thoon and Anabesineus,
and Amphialus, son of Polyneus son of Tecton;
and up rose also Euryalus, equal to man-slaying Ares,
son of Naubolus, who was the best in looks and form
of all the Phaeacians after blameless Laodamas.
And up stood the three sons of blameless Alcinous,
Laodamas and Halius and godlike Clytoneus.
These first tried themselves in a foot-race.
For them the course was stretched from the turning-post; and all together
they flew swiftly, raising the dust of the plain;
and of them far the best at running was blameless Clytoneus;
as far as the cast of mules in a fallow field,
so far running out ahead he reached the throng, and the others were left behind.
And they tried themselves at painful wrestling;
in this Euryalus surpassed all the best.
In leaping Amphialus was the foremost of all;
and with the discus Elatreus was by far the best of all,
and in boxing Laodamas, the good son of Alcinous.
But when all had delighted their hearts with the contests,
Laodamas, son of Alcinous, spoke among them:

Come, friends, let us ask the stranger whether he knows
134	and has learned any contest. In build he is not bad,
135	in thighs and calves and both arms above,
136	and strong neck and great strength; nor does he lack youth,
137	but he is broken by many troubles;
138	for I say there is nothing worse than the sea
139	to confound a man, even if he is very strong.
Then Euryalus answered him and spoke:

Laodamas, you have spoken this word very rightly.
142	Go yourself now and challenge him and tell him the word.
And when the good son of Alcinous heard this,
he went and stood in the midst and addressed Odysseus:

Come, father stranger, you too, try the contests,
146	if you have learned any; and it is fitting that you know contests;
147	for there is no greater fame for a man as long as he lives
148	than what he achieves with his feet and his hands.
149	But come, try, and scatter the cares from your heart.
150	Your journey will not long be far off, but already
151	the ship is drawn down and the companions are ready.
Answering him, Odysseus of many wiles said:

Laodamas, why do you bid me this, mocking me?
154	Cares are more in my mind than contests,
155	who before suffered very much and toiled much,
156	and now among your assembly I sit, in need of a return,
157	beseeching the king and all the people.
Then Euryalus answered him and rebuked him to his face:

No, stranger, I do not liken you to a man skilled
160	in contests, such as are many among men,
161	but to one who, going to and fro with a many-benched ship,
162	is a leader of sailors who are traders,
163	mindful of cargo and a watcher over outward-bound freight
164	and greedy gains; you do not look like an athlete.
Looking darkly at him, Odysseus of many wiles said:

Stranger, you have not spoken well; you seem a reckless man.
167	So the gods do not give gracious gifts to all
168	men, neither in form nor in mind nor in speech.
169	For one man is poorer in looks,
170	but a god crowns his shape with words, and they look on him
171	delighted; and he speaks without stumbling,
172	with sweet modesty, and stands out among those assembled,
173	and as he goes through the city they look on him as on a god.
174	And another again is like the immortals in looks,
175	but no grace is wreathed about his words,
176	as with you too the looks are outstanding, nor could a god
177	make them otherwise, but in mind you are empty.
178	You have stirred the heart in my dear breast
179	by speaking not in due order. I am not unskilled in contests,
180	as you say, but I think I was among the first,
181	while I trusted in my youth and in my hands.
182	But now I am held by misery and pains; for I endured much,
183	the wars of men and the painful waves, in making trial of them.
184	But even so, though I have suffered many evils, I will try the contests;
185	for your word bites the heart, and you have urged me by speaking.
He spoke, and leapt up with his cloak still on, and took a discus
larger and thick, heavier by no small amount
than that with which the Phaeacians threw against one another.
This he whirled and let fly from his stout hand,
and the stone hummed; and they crouched to the ground,
the long-oared Phaeacians, ship-famed men,
under the rush of the stone; and it flew past the marks of all,
running lightly from his hand. And Athena set the mark,
likened to a man, and spoke a word and called him by name:

Even a blind man, stranger, could distinguish your mark,
196	feeling for it, for it is not mixed in with the crowd,
197	but is far first. And you take heart in this contest;
198	none of the Phaeacians will reach this or surpass it.
So she spoke, and much-enduring godlike Odysseus rejoiced,
glad that he saw a kindly companion in the contest.
And then more lightly he spoke among the Phaeacians:

Reach this now, young men. Soon afterwards another
203	I think I will throw as far, or even farther.
204	And of the others whomever heart and spirit bid,
205	come, let him try, since you have angered me greatly,
206	either at boxing or wrestling or even running, I do not begrudge it,
207	any of the Phaeacians, except Laodamas himself.
208	For he is my host; who would fight with one who treats him kindly?
209	Senseless indeed and worthless is that man
210	who offers his host a challenge in contests
211	in a foreign land; he cuts short all his own interests.
212	Of the others I refuse none and slight none,
213	but I wish to know them and to try them face to face.
214	For I am not bad at anything, among men, in all contests;
215	well I know how to handle the polished bow;
216	I would be first to hit my man shooting among a crowd
217	of hostile men, even if many companions
218	stood near and shot arrows at men.
219	Only Philoctetes surpassed me with the bow
220	in the land of the Trojans, when we Achaeans shot.
221	Of the others I say I am far the better,
222	as many mortals as now eat bread upon the earth.
223	But with men of former times I will not wish to contend,
224	neither with Heracles nor with Eurytus of Oechalia,
225	who even contended with the immortals about the bow.
226	Therefore great Eurytus died quickly, and did not come to old age
227	in his halls; for Apollo, angered,
228	killed him, because he challenged him to a shooting-match.
229	With the spear I throw as far as no other with an arrow.
230	Only in running I fear that one of the Phaeacians
231	may pass me; for I was shamefully worn down
232	by many waves, since provision on the ship
233	was not ample; therefore my limbs are loosened.
So he spoke, and they all became silent in stillness.
Alcinous alone answered him and said:

Stranger, since you do not speak ungracefully among us,
237	but wish to show your excellence, which attends you,
238	angry that this man, standing by you in the contest,
239	rebuked you, so that no mortal would find fault with your excellence,
240	whoever knew how to speak fittingly in his mind;
241	but come now, understand my word, that you may also tell another
242	of the heroes, when in your halls
243	you feast beside your wife and children,
244	remembering our excellence, what works Zeus
245	has set for us continually from our fathers' time.
246	For we are not blameless boxers nor wrestlers,
247	but we run swiftly with our feet and are best in ships,
248	and always dear to us are the feast and the lyre and dances
249	and changes of clothes and hot baths and beds.
250	But come, whoever are the best dancers of the Phaeacians,
251	play, that the stranger may tell his friends,
252	returning home, how far we excel others
253	in seafaring and running and dancing and song.
254	And let someone go quickly and bring the clear-toned lyre
255	to Demodocus, which lies somewhere in our house.
So spoke godlike Alcinous, and the herald rose
to bring the hollow lyre from the king's house.
And nine chosen stewards, all from the people, stood up,
who arranged each thing well at the games,
and levelled a dancing-floor, and widened the fair ring.
And the herald came near bringing the clear-toned lyre
to Demodocus; and he went into the middle; and around him youths
in their first youth stood, skilled in dancing,
and struck the divine dancing-floor with their feet. And Odysseus
watched the flashing of their feet, and marvelled in his heart.
And he, playing the lyre, struck up a fair song
about the love of Ares and fair-crowned Aphrodite,
how first they lay together in the house of Hephaestus
in secret, and he gave many gifts, and shamed the bed and couch
of lord Hephaestus. At once a messenger came to him,
the Sun, who had noticed them mingling in love.
And when Hephaestus heard the heart-grieving word,
he went to his smithy, devising evils in his mind,
and set the great anvil on the anvil-block, and hammered out bonds
unbreakable, not to be loosed, that they might stay fast there.
But when he had made the trap, angry with Ares,
he went to the chamber, where his dear bed lay,
and poured the bonds round about the bedposts on all sides;
and many hung down from above from the roof-beams,
like fine spider-webs, which no one could even see,
not even of the blessed gods; for they were made exceedingly cunning.
But when he had poured all the trap round the bed,
he pretended to go to Lemnos, the well-built citadel,
which is by far the dearest of all lands to him.
And Ares of the golden reins kept no blind watch,
when he saw Hephaestus, famed for his art, going away;
he went to the house of far-famed Hephaestus,
longing for the love of fair-crowned Cytherea.
And she, having newly come from her father, mighty son of Cronos,
had sat down; and he came into the house,
and clung to her hand, and spoke a word and called her by name:
So he spoke, and to her sleeping seemed welcome.
And the two went to the bed and lay down; and around them the bonds,
the cunning work of crafty Hephaestus, poured,
and they could not move or lift any of their limbs.
And then they knew that there was no longer escape.
And near them came the far-famed lame god,
having turned back before he reached the land of Lemnos;
for the Sun kept the watch for him and told him the word.
He went to his house, grieved in his dear heart;
and he stood in the forecourt, and fierce anger seized him;
and he cried out terribly, and called to all the gods:

Father Zeus and you other blessed gods who are for ever,
307	come here, that you may see deeds laughable and not to be borne,
308	how Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus, always dishonours me, lame as I am,
309	and loves destructive Ares,
310	because he is handsome and sound of foot, but I
311	was born weak. Yet no other is to blame for me,
312	but my two parents, whom I wish had never begotten me.
313	But you shall see where these two sleep in love
314	having gone to my bed, and I am grieved as I look.
315	I do not expect they will lie thus even for a little while,
316	though they love each other much; soon neither will wish
317	to sleep; but my trap and bond will hold them,
318	until her father pays back to me all the bride-gifts,
319	as many as I gave him for the sake of the shameless girl,
320	because his daughter is fair, but not self-controlled.
So he spoke, and the gods gathered at the bronze-floored house;
Poseidon the earth-holder came, and came the helper
Hermes, and came the lord far-working Apollo.
But the female goddesses stayed at home out of modesty, each.
And the gods stood in the forecourt, givers of good things;
and unquenchable laughter arose among the blessed gods
as they looked on the arts of crafty Hephaestus.
And thus one would say, looking at his neighbour:

Evil deeds do not prosper; the slow catches the swift,
330	as now Hephaestus, slow though he is, has caught Ares,
331	who is the swiftest of the gods who hold Olympus,
332	lame though he is, by art; and he owes the adulterer's fine.
So they spoke such things to one another;
and lord Apollo, son of Zeus, said to Hermes:

Hermes, son of Zeus, guide, giver of good things,
336	would you be willing, pressed by strong bonds,
337	to sleep in the bed beside golden Aphrodite?
Then the guide, the slayer of Argus, answered him:

Would that this might be, lord far-shooting Apollo;
340	let bonds three times as many, endless, hold me round about,
341	and you gods and all the goddesses look on,
342	but let me sleep beside golden Aphrodite.
So he spoke, and laughter arose among the immortal gods.
But Poseidon laughter did not seize, and he kept beseeching
Hephaestus, famed for his works, to release Ares;
and speaking to him he addressed him with winged words:

Release him; and I promise you, as you bid,
348	that he will pay all that is due among the immortal gods.
Then again the far-famed lame god said to him:

Do not bid me this, Poseidon earth-holder;
351	wretched are pledges for the wretched to pledge.
352	How could I bind you among the immortal gods,
353	if Ares should go away, escaping both debt and bond?
Then again Poseidon the Earth-shaker said to him:

Hephaestus, even if Ares, escaping the debt,
356	should go off in flight, I myself will pay you this.
Then the far-famed lame god answered him:
It is not possible, nor is it fitting, to refuse your word.
So saying, the strength of Hephaestus loosed the bond.
And they, when they were loosed from the bond, strong though it was,
at once leaping up, he went off to Thrace,
and she came to Cyprus, laughter-loving Aphrodite,
to Paphos; there she has a precinct and a fragrant altar.
There the Graces bathed her and anointed her with oil
ambrosial, such as clothes the gods who are for ever,
and put lovely clothes about her, a wonder to behold.
This the far-famed singer sang; and Odysseus
took delight in his heart listening, and so did the others,
the long-oared Phaeacians, ship-famed men.
And Alcinous bade Halius and Laodamas
dance alone, since no one contended with them.
And they, when they had taken a fair ball in their hands,
a purple one, which prudent Polybus made for them,
one of them would throw it up to the shadowy clouds,
bending backwards, and the other, leaping high from the ground,
would easily catch it, before his feet touched the floor.
And when they had tried the ball straight upward,
they danced then on the much-nourishing earth,
often changing places; and the other youths clapped
standing about the ring, and a great din rose beneath.
Then godlike Odysseus addressed Alcinous:

Lord Alcinous, most renowned of all the people,
383	you boasted that your dancers were the best,
384	and indeed it has been made good; awe holds me as I look.
So he spoke, and the sacred might of Alcinous rejoiced,
and at once he spoke among the Phaeacians, lovers of oars:

Hear me, leaders and counsellors of the Phaeacians.
388	The stranger seems to me to be very wise.
389	But come, let us give him a guest-gift, as is fitting.
390	For twelve outstanding kings in the district
391	rule as leaders, and I myself am the thirteenth;
392	of these let each of you bring a well-washed cloak and a tunic
393	and a talent of precious gold.
394	And let us bring everything quickly together, that in his hands
395	the stranger may have it and go to supper rejoicing in his heart.
396	And let Euryalus himself make amends to him with words
397	and a gift, since he did not speak a word according to what is right.
So he spoke, and they all approved and bade,
and each sent a herald to bring gifts.
Then Euryalus answered him and spoke:

Lord Alcinous, most renowned of all the people,
402	therefore I will make amends to the stranger, as you bid.
403	I will give him this sword all of bronze, on which the hilt
404	is silver, and a sheath of newly sawn ivory
405	is wrapped about it; and it will be worth much to him.
So saying he put the silver-studded sword in his hands
and speaking to him addressed him with winged words:

Hail, father stranger; and if any word has been said
409	that was dreadful, may the storm-winds at once seize it and carry it off.
410	And may the gods grant you to see your wife and reach your native land,
411	since long you suffer woes far from your friends.
Answering him, Odysseus of many wiles said:

And you, friend, hail greatly, and may the gods grant you happiness.
414	And may there be no longing for this sword hereafter for you,
415	which you have given me, making amends with words.
He spoke, and slung the silver-studded sword about his shoulders.
And the sun set, and the famous gifts were at hand for him.
And these the noble heralds carried to the house of Alcinous;
and the sons of blameless Alcinous received them
and set the very beautiful gifts beside their revered mother.
And the sacred might of Alcinous led them,
and coming they sat down on the high seats.
Then the might of Alcinous said to Arete:

Come here, woman, bring a chest, outstanding, whichever is best;
425	and put in it yourself a well-washed cloak and a tunic.
426	And heat a bronze cauldron on the fire for him, and warm water,
427	that having bathed and seen all the gifts
428	well laid out, which the blameless Phaeacians brought here,
429	he may take delight in the feast and in hearing the hymn of song.
430	And I will give him this very beautiful goblet of mine,
431	of gold, that remembering me all his days
432	he may pour libations in his hall to Zeus and the other gods.
So he spoke, and Arete told her maids
to set a great tripod on the fire as quickly as possible.
And they set the bath-water tripod on the blazing fire,
and poured in water, and taking wood kindled it beneath.
The fire licked the belly of the tripod, and the water was warmed;
meanwhile Arete brought out for the stranger a very beautiful chest
from the chamber, and put in it the fair gifts,
clothing and gold, which the Phaeacians gave him;
and she herself put in a cloak and a fair tunic,
and speaking to him she addressed him with winged words:

Look at the lid yourself now, and quickly fasten the knot,
444	lest anyone harm you on the way, when you
445	sleep sweet sleep, going in the black ship.
And when much-enduring godlike Odysseus heard this,
at once he fitted on the lid, and quickly fastened the knot,
intricate, which once queenly Circe had taught him in his mind.
And at once the housekeeper bade him go bathe,
going to the bath; and he saw it gladly in his heart,
the hot bath, since he had not been used to such care,
ever since he left the house of fair-haired Calypso.
For there his care had been continual, as a god's.
And when the maids had bathed him and anointed him with oil,
and cast about him a fair cloak and a tunic,
coming out of the bath he went to the men drinking wine;
and Nausicaa, having beauty from the gods,
stood by the post of the well-made roof,
and marvelled at Odysseus, seeing him with her eyes,
and speaking to him she addressed him with winged words:

Hail, stranger, that sometime when you are in your native land
462	you may remember me, because to me first you owe the price of saving your life.
Answering her, Odysseus of many wiles said:

Nausicaa, daughter of great-hearted Alcinous,
465	so may Zeus now grant, loud-thundering husband of Hera,
466	that I come home and see the day of return;
467	then even there I would pray to you as to a god
468	always, all my days; for you gave me life, maiden.
He spoke, and sat on a chair beside king Alcinous;
and they were already distributing portions and mixing wine.
And the herald came near leading the beloved singer,
Demodocus, honoured by the people; and he seated him
in the midst of the banqueters, leaning him against a tall pillar.
Then Odysseus of many wiles said to the herald,
cutting off a piece from the chine, and much more was left,
of a white-tusked swine, and rich fat was on both sides:

Herald, here, give this meat, that he may eat,
478	to Demodocus; and I will greet him, grieved though I am;
479	for among all men on earth singers
480	have a share of honour and reverence, because
481	the Muse taught them songs, and loves the tribe of singers.
So he spoke, and the herald took it and put it in the hands
of the hero Demodocus; and he received it, and rejoiced in his heart.
And they stretched out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
But when they had put away the desire for drink and food,
then Odysseus of many wiles said to Demodocus:

Demodocus, I praise you exceedingly above all mortals.
488	Either the Muse, child of Zeus, taught you, or Apollo;
489	for very rightly you sing the fate of the Achaeans,
490	all that the Achaeans did and suffered and toiled,
491	as if you yourself were present or heard from another.
492	But come now, change your theme and sing the building of the wooden
493	horse, which Epeius made with Athena,
494	which once as a trick godlike Odysseus brought into the citadel,
495	having filled it with men who sacked Ilios.
496	If you tell me this rightly,
497	at once I will tell all men
498	that a kindly god has granted you inspired song.
So he spoke, and he, stirred by the god, began, and showed his song,
taking it from the point where some, on their well-benched ships,
having set fire to the huts, sailed away,
the Argives, and the others already around famous Odysseus
sat in the assembly of the Trojans, hidden in the horse;
for the Trojans themselves had dragged it to the citadel.
So it stood, and they, sitting around it, said many confused things;
and a threefold counsel pleased them,
either to cleave the hollow timber with pitiless bronze,
or to drag it to the top and throw it down the rocks,
or to let it be a great offering to charm the gods,
as indeed it was afterwards to be accomplished;
for it was fate to perish when the city should enclose
the great wooden horse, where all the best of the Argives sat
bringing slaughter and doom to the Trojans.
And he sang how the sons of the Achaeans sacked the city,
pouring out of the horse, leaving the hollow ambush.
And he sang how they laid waste the steep city, one here and another there,
and how Odysseus went to the house of Deiphobus,
like Ares, with godlike Menelaus.
There, he said, daring the most dreadful fight
he won, and afterwards through great-hearted Athena.
This the far-famed singer sang; and Odysseus
melted, and tears wetted his cheeks beneath his eyelids.
As a woman weeps, falling about her dear husband,
who has fallen before his own city and people,
warding off the pitiless day from the town and his children;
she, seeing him dying and gasping,
clings about him and wails shrilly; and the men behind her,
striking her back and shoulders with spears,
lead her into slavery, to have toil and misery;
and with most pitiable grief her cheeks waste away;
so Odysseus shed a pitiable tear beneath his brows.
Then from all the others he escaped notice shedding tears,
but Alcinous alone noticed him and observed,
sitting near him, and heard him groaning heavily.
At once he spoke among the Phaeacians, lovers of oars:

Hear me, leaders and counsellors of the Phaeacians,
537	and let Demodocus now hold back the clear-toned lyre;
538	for he does not sing this in a way pleasing to all.
539	Since we have been at supper and the divine singer was roused,
540	since then he has not yet ceased from mournful lament,
541	the stranger; surely grief has come over his mind.
542	But come, let him hold back, that we may all delight alike,
543	hosts and guest, since it is much fairer so;
544	for on account of the revered stranger all this has been made ready,
545	the escort and the dear gifts, which we give in friendship.
546	In place of a brother a stranger and suppliant is made
547	to a man who touches even a little on understanding.
548	Therefore do not you either hide with shrewd thoughts
549	whatever I shall ask you; it is fairer for you to say.
550	Tell the name by which they called you there, your mother and father
551	and the others in the town and those who live around.
552	For no one of men is wholly nameless,
553	neither base nor noble, once he is born,
554	but parents give names to all, when they have borne them.
555	And tell me your land, your people and your city,
556	that the ships may take you there, steering by their own minds;
557	for the Phaeacians have no helmsmen,
558	nor are there any steering-oars, which other ships have;
559	but the ships themselves know the thoughts and minds of men,
560	and they know the cities and rich fields of all
561	men, and they cross the gulf of the sea most swiftly,
562	wrapped in mist and cloud; nor ever for them
563	is there fear either of being harmed or of perishing.
564	But this I once heard my father say,
565	Nausithous, who said that Poseidon was jealous
566	of us, because we are unharmed escorts of all.
567	He said that some day a well-built ship of Phaeacian men,
568	returning from an escort on the misty sea,
569	he would shatter, and would cover our city with a great mountain.
570	So the old man spoke; and the god may either accomplish this
571	or leave it unaccomplished, as is dear to his heart.
572	But come, tell me this, and relate it exactly,
573	where you wandered, and to what lands of men you came,
574	both the people themselves and their well-inhabited cities,

580	for men, that there might be a song for those to come.

582	a good man, a son-in-law or father-in-law, who are the nearest
583	after one's own blood and race?
584	Or some companion, a man who knew kindly ways,
